name: Threat detection (SIEM)
summary: Collecting security logs from many systems in one place and running detection rules over them, so that suspicious activity becomes an alert an analyst can act on.
howItWorks: Agents and connectors ship security-relevant logs to one place: cloud audit trails such as AWS CloudTrail, Windows event logs, sign-ins from an identity provider, firewall and DNS logs. A parser turns each line into named fields, and a rule engine runs detection rules over the stream. The simplest rule matches a single event: a CloudTrail call made with the AWS root user, or `whoami.exe` started with `/all`. A correlation rule looks across a time window, grouped by a field such as user or host: 10 or more failed logons by one user within 10 minutes, followed by a successful one. Rules run either on each event as it arrives or as a scheduled query over a lookback window; Microsoft Sentinel’s scheduled rules, for example, run every 5 minutes to every 14 days. A match becomes an alert with a severity and tags, such as the MITRE ATT&CK technique it points to, and goes to an analyst to triage, while the raw logs stay stored for investigations and hunts. Each SIEM has its own query language (KQL in Sentinel, YARA-L in Google Security Operations, SPL in Splunk), so a rule written for one doesn’t run on another. Shared rule formats fix that. A Sigma rule is written once in YAML against generic field names and a log source such as `product: windows`, `category: process_creation`; pySigma backends then convert it into each SIEM’s query, with processing pipelines mapping the field names, or an engine such as RSigma evaluates it directly on the event stream.
analogy: A security desk in a large building. Cameras and badge readers on every floor feed one wall of screens. The guard keeps a short list of things to watch for (“the same badge failing at a door ten times, then opening it”, “anyone in the server room at 3 a.m.”) and calls for help only when one of them happens. A shared rulebook lets guards in other buildings, with other camera brands, watch for the same things.
useWhen: Attacks show up only in logs: credentials used from an unusual place, root or admin accounts used directly, a system process started from an odd directory
Activity is spread across many systems, so one event looks harmless and only the sequence means something, such as many failed logins and then a success
Regulations such as PCI DSS or HIPAA expect security events to be logged and reviewed centrally
You run more than one SIEM, or may switch: keep rules in Sigma and convert them instead of maintaining a copy per query language
avoidWhen: Collecting every log with no rules or owner: a SIEM only finds what its rules look for, and alerts nobody reads protect nobody

Treating a managed detection service as a SIEM: Amazon GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail, VPC flow and DNS logs with AWS’s threat intelligence and ML models, then discards those logs, so they aren’t kept for your own searches

Assuming a converted rule behaves the same everywhere: field names and log sources differ between data sets, so conversion needs a pipeline that maps them, and some Sigma modifiers, such as `re` for regular expressions, only work where the backend supports them
example: A company forwards the Windows Security event log from its servers to its SIEM and keeps its detections in Git as Sigma YAML, following the example in the Sigma correlation specification. Rule `failed_login` matches event ID 4625 (529 on old systems); rule `successful_login` matches 4624 (or 528). An `event_count` correlation counts `failed_login` events per `User` and fires at 10 or more within 10 minutes. A `temporal_ordered` correlation, at level high, fires when that is followed by a successful login for the same user in the same 10-minute window: a password guessed by brute force. CI converts them with `sigma convert` into the SIEM’s query language. Ordinary logons match nothing. One account with 14 failures and then a success raises a single high-severity alert, which an analyst picks up, while the individual failed logons stay in storage for the investigation.

providers.aws: Amazon GuardDuty (managed threat detection over CloudTrail management events, VPC flow logs and DNS logs; Extended Threat Detection for multi-stage attack sequences); AWS Security Hub CSPM gathers findings from GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie; Amazon Security Lake centralizes security logs in your own S3 buckets as Parquet in the OCSF schema
providers.gcp: Google Security Operations (Google SecOps, formerly Chronicle): YARA-L 2.0 rules over normalized UDM events, single-event or multi-event with a `match` time window; curated detections
providers.azure: Microsoft Sentinel: scheduled analytics rules, each a KQL query run every 5 minutes to 14 days over a lookback window, with an alert threshold; rule templates from Microsoft and solution vendors
providers.oss: Sigma rules (converted with pySigma and sigma-cli, or evaluated by RSigma); Wazuh (3,000+ built-in rules and decoders); Falco (YAML rules over Linux syscalls, a CNCF graduated project); source-available: Elastic Security’s detection-rules repo (Elastic License v2)

sections.title: One idea, many rule languages
sections.intro: Every SIEM runs detection rules over stored or streaming events, but each writes them in its own language. Sigma sits across them as a shared format.

rows.label: Sigma

Any log source, after conversion to a SIEM query or in an engine such as RSigma

sections.title: Detection as code
body: Rules are small text files, so teams keep them in Git and review changes like code. Elastic said in 2020 that it had moved its rules to a repository with automated tests that validate query syntax, schema use and metadata on every contribution. Sigma’s own site pitches the same workflow: version control over detections and deployment from a CI/CD pipeline straight into the SIEM.

There are two ways to run a shared rule. Conversion turns it into the target’s own query: `sigma convert -t splunk -p sysmon rules/` uses a backend for the query language and a processing pipeline that maps Sigma’s generic field names, such as `CommandLine`, to the names in your data. Direct evaluation skips the SIEM query language: an engine such as RSigma compiles the rules into matchers, applies the same kind of pipeline and checks each event as it arrives, keeping correlation windows in memory.

Tests close the loop. A rule should fire on a known-bad sample and stay quiet on a day of normal traffic. RSigma’s `rule backtest` replays event files against per-rule expectations and writes a JUnit report for CI, and its linter checks rules against the Sigma specification before they ship.

story: Security log tools were first sold as two kinds of product: security information management (SIM), for long-term storage, analysis and reporting of log data, and security event management (SEM), for real-time monitoring, correlation of events and notifications. In 2005, Gartner analysts Mark Nicolett and Amrit Williams named the combination security information and event management (SIEM). NIST later defined a SIEM tool as an application that gathers security data from information system components and presents it as actionable information through a single interface.

For years the detection logic stayed locked inside each product, in its own query language. Florian Roth and Thomas Patzke felt that pain while handling incidents: good searches could not be shared with teams on other SIEMs. Roth committed the first Sigma rules on December 24, 2016, the two refined the format for two to three months, and Sigma was released in 2017 as a generic YAML signature format for log events, with a converter to SIEM queries. Its README puts it this way: “Sigma is for log files what Snort is for network traffic and YARA is for files.”

Detection as code followed. In June 2020, Elastic opened its detection rules to the public as TOML files with automated tests. Sigma’s specification 2.0 (August 2024) replaced the old aggregation expressions with correlation rules, and the `sigmac` converter was retired in favor of pySigma. Cloud providers built their own detection services and rule languages, such as YARA-L in Google Security Operations and KQL analytics rules in Microsoft Sentinel, while open engines such as RSigma (2026) evaluate Sigma rules directly on a stream.

choices.choice: Generic log sources and field names, mapped later
choices.why: A Sigma rule names a log source such as `category: process_creation` instead of Sysmon, Windows Security auditing and every other product-specific source. The specification calls this abstraction the advantage: the rule isn’t tied to one telemetry source, and converters map it to indexes and fields.

choices.choice: Simple searches and a few common correlations, not a full query language
choices.why: Sigma’s design philosophy trades expressiveness for portability: basic searches and a few common correlations (such as counts) cover more than 90% of day-to-day detection needs, and keeping to them means a detection can be shared across all sorts of security environments.

choices.choice: Correlations as separate rules that reference other rules
choices.why: A correlation names the rules it counts or orders, so correlations can be chained, and single matches can stay low or informational while the correlation raises the level.
Sigma chose YAML because it is easy to read and write; files in Git get version control, review and deployment through CI/CD, the same path Elastic took for its rules in 2020.
